records.cool_rest_note: Can be overwintered indoors by keeping it dormant: kept very dry and watered only sparingly (when it shows signs of wilting) until after the danger of frost has passed, at which point normal watering resumes.
unknowns: humidity_need / humidity_pct_min / humidity_pct_max: no source states a humidity preference level; Clemson's indoor factsheet only warns that overwatering combined with high humidity causes oedema (corky leaf spots), a caution rather than a stated need.

chill_damage_f: no source gives an actionable frost/cold damage-onset temperature. RHS lists a hardiness rating H2 ('tolerant of low temperatures, but not surviving being frozen', 1-5 degrees C) but this is a survival/tolerance classification for an established plant, not a damage-onset threshold, so it was not mapped to this field.
soil_ph_min / soil_ph_max: Missouri Botanical Garden and RHS describe pH only qualitatively ('neutral to slightly alkaline' / 'Neutral or Alkaline'); no cited source gives a numeric pH range.
light_fc_min / light_fc_good: all cited outdoor sources give sun exposure as a duration/category (full sun, part shade) rather than a footcandle intensity value; no source states footcandles.

direct_sun_hours_max: sources give a minimum sun requirement (at least 4-6 hours) and a general full-sun-to-part-shade range, but none states a maximum number of direct-sun hours the plant tolerates before needing protection.

fertilize_interval_days: sources give two different, context-specific cadences (outdoor beds: every 4-6 weeks; indoor containers: semi-monthly) that don't reduce to one clean day count without arbitrarily picking a context, so left null.
fertilize_strength: no source specifies a full/half/quarter-strength dilution for fertilizer application.
water_check_depth_cm: Clemson's indoor factsheet gives a check depth in inches (4 to 6 inches) but not centimeters; declined to convert an inch range into a single cm figure.

water_growing_days_est / water_dormant_days_est / water_estimate_basis: sources describe watering only qualitatively ('water regularly, allow to dry between waterings'; during dormancy 'water sparingly, only when...wilting') without a specific day interval to build a defensible estimate.

scientific_name_accepted — removed on audit: The record sets this to "Pelargonium x hybridum" on the strength of a single admissible source (NC State Plant Toolbox: "Previously known as: Pelargonium x hortorum" / "This name is now a synonym of P. x hybridum"), but I fetched the record's other cited admissible sources directly and found a genuine cross-source conflict the record resolved by picking a value instead of leaving it as the given name or flagging the uncertainty: RHS's own structured 'Name Status' field for Pelargonium x hortorum reads 'Unresolved' (confirmed live) -- RHS, which is in the business of tracking nomenclature status, explicitly does not confirm hortorum has been superseded. Meanwhile Clemson HGIC (confirmed: 'The page mentions Pelargonium x hortorum specifically as the scientific name'), Missouri Botanical Garden (confirmed: page header text 'Pelargonium x hortorum'), and UF/IFAS (confirmed: 'The page uses Pelargonium x hortorum') all still use hortorum as the live, current operative name in their own text. One extension database's internal relabeling was treated as settling a taxonomic question that four other admissible sources, including the actual nomenclature-status source (RHS), do not agree is settled.

name_note — removed on audit: The note's own body accurately lists the contradicting evidence (RHS 'Unresolved'; Clemson/MBG/RHS/UF-IFAS all still using hortorum) but its final sentence still concludes 'Pelargonium x hybridum is recorded here as the accepted name' -- the note undermines its own conclusion. Given RHS explicitly declines to resolve the name status, a plant-database synonym note from one extension site is not sufficient grounds to declare a different accepted name over the given one.

toxicity_detail — removed on audit: The field states 'Listed as a problem for dogs, cats, and horses, and poisonous to humans,' and its supporting citation's claim label repeats 'problem for cats, dogs, and horses.' But the quote text actually attached to that citation ("Poison Severity: Low Poison Symptoms: Vomiting, anorexia... Poison Toxic Principle: Geraniol, linalool Causes Contact Dermatitis: Yes Poison Part: Leaves") never mentions dogs, horses, or humans anywhere -- only 'Cats are most sensitive' appears, which is a comparative remark, not a species listing. The claim outruns its own quoted evidence. (I independently fetched the live NC State page and it does carry a separate 'Problem For: Cat, Dog, Horse / Poisonous to Human' structured section, so the assertion is probably true in substance -- but the citation as constructed in this record does not establish it, which is the defect the audit is checking for.)

water_regime — removed on audit: Missouri Botanical Garden's Plant Finder page -- already cited three times elsewhere in this record -- carries a structured 'Water: Medium' rating and a separate Culture-section sentence 'Water regularly throughout growing season' (both confirmed by direct fetch), neither of which appears anywhere in this record's citations. MBG's 'Medium' water category denotes consistent/regular moisture, not a deliberate dry-down cycle, and sits in tension with the 'dry_surface_between' value the record built from Clemson/NC State/RHS's 'allow soil to dry between waterings' language. This is exactly the scenario the audit's structural check #1 calls out: a cited source's own structured field was never checked against the prose actually quoted, on a harm-capable field. water_dry_down_target inherits the same unreconciled conflict since it's built on the same determination.

chill_damage_f: sources call it a tender/tropical annual that 'will not tolerate cold weather' and instruct planting after last frost / bringing plants indoors before first frost, but none states the specific temperature at which cold damage begins (an RHS H1B hardiness rating implies a general 10-15°C/50-59°F winter-protection category but is not a stated damage-onset figure, so it was not used).

direct_sun_hours_max: NC State's Light attribute defines 'Partial Shade' as '2-6 hours' of direct sun, but this is the site's generic category definition reused across plant profiles, not a species-specific hours-of-direct-sun tolerance figure, so it was not used.
soil_base: sources describe soil texture, pH, and drainage traits but none names a specific growing-medium/potting-mix category.

soil_drainage: sources consistently pair 'well-drained' with 'moist' (NC State's own structured Soil Drainage field lists both 'Good Drainage' and 'Moist' together) without using a fast/moderate/moisture-retentive style term, so no enum value was assigned.

soil_ph_min — removed on audit: Derived from NC State's structured tag 'Soil pH: Neutral (6.0-8.0)'. Verified by direct fetch that this exact bucket string -- 'Acid (<6.0) Neutral (6.0-8.0)' -- appears verbatim on completely unrelated NC State plant pages (Hosta spp., Rosa spp.). It is the site's fixed, generic definition of what the 'Neutral' pH category means, not a value measured or curated for Impatiens walleriana specifically. The record's own unknowns section already applies exactly this skepticism to a different NC State bucket field (direct_sun_hours_max: 'the site's generic category definition reused across plant profiles, not a species-specific... figure, so it was not used') but failed to apply the same reasoning to soil pH. Compounding this, the same NC State page's own prose -- quoted elsewhere in this record's own water citation -- says the plant needs 'a slightly acidic pH,' which is inconsistent with a 6.0-8.0 (neutral-to-alkaline) range. This is the structural-check-1 pattern (a cited source's own structured field contradicts its own prose) using a value that is also generic boilerplate rather than species-specific data. Should be null, not 6.

soil_ph_max — removed on audit: Same defect as soil_ph_min: the '8.0' upper bound comes from NC State's site-wide generic 'Neutral (6.0-8.0)' bucket label, confirmed via direct fetch to be identical boilerplate on unrelated plant pages (Hosta spp., Rosa spp.), not species-specific data -- and it conflicts with the same source's own prose describing the plant as needing 'a slightly acidic pH,' which the record itself quotes elsewhere. Should be null, not 8.

outdoor_sun_exposure — removed on audit: The 'full_sun' element in this array is supported by only one of the four admissible sources cited (RHS, a UK-climate source), and even that source's own prose conditions it explicitly: 'will also thrive in full sun if kept moist and well watered.' A second RHS citation ('Position Full shade, Full sun, Partial shade') is used to back full_sun without carrying that condition into the record. Meanwhile the other three admissible sources all cap this species at part shade to full shade and actively warn against full sun: NC State says 'too much sun may scorch the leaves,' MOBOT says 'Sun: Part shade to full shade,' and Clemson says old-fashioned impatiens (this species) 'must have protection from hot afternoon sun to maintain their colors.' Storing an unconditioned 'full_sun' value when 3 of 4 admissible sources warn against it, and the 4th only supports it with an unstored moisture caveat, overstates what the evidence collectively supports and risks the plant being sited somewhere it will scorch.

water_regime: genuine cross-source disagreement. Clemson's own text calls for keeping soil 'evenly moist' while plants establish but then watering established plants 'deeply once per week, allowing the soil to dry somewhat between watering'; Penn State separately advises letting soil 'dry slightly between each watering'; Missouri Botanical Garden's structured field reads 'Water: Medium' next to its own prose calling the ideal soil 'evenly moist.' These do not converge on a single keep_moist vs. dry_surface_between regime, so left null rather than pick a side.

water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, water_check_depth_cm, water_dry_down_target, water_estimate_basis: left null because any specific interval would silently resolve the same water_regime disagreement noted above; only Clemson gives a concrete number ('about an inch of water per week' / 'once per week' once established), and using it alone would misrepresent the conflict as settled.

fertilize_interval_days, fertilize_strength, fertilize_active_months: Clemson describes only a single application, 'a slow-release fertilizer formulated for annuals can be incorporated at the time of planting' — not a recurring interval, a strength/dilution, or specific active months — so left null.

toxic_to_pets, toxicity_detail: no admissible source states pet-specific toxicity for Tagetes patula. NC State's Tagetes genus page (covering four species together, not patula specifically) describes toxicity to humans only — contact dermatitis from sap plus sunlight, and harm if eaten 'in large amounts' — with no mention of pets or animals, so no value was taken for this field rather than inferring pet toxicity from a genus-level, human-only source.

is_houseplant is recorded false based on the three species-specific sources (Clemson, Missouri Botanical Garden, RHS), which describe only outdoor garden/bedding/container use; NC State's Tagetes genus page separately lists 'Houseplant or interiorscape' and 'Houseplants' among general genus uses, but that is stated for the genus (T. erecta, T. lucida, T. patula, T. tenuifolia together) rather than for T. patula specifically, so it was not treated as support for true.

is_houseplant — removed on audit: Record asserts false based only on absence of houseplant framing in three sources (MOBOT sowing instructions, RHS 'Bedding' tag, Clemson garden-bed prep) — a negative claim built from absence of evidence, not a source stating T. patula is never grown indoors. Meanwhile the record's own cited NC State Extension page (plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/tagetes/common-name/marigold/, admissible domain, already used elsewhere in this record for the toxicity citation) carries structured fields directly on point: 'Uses (Ethnobotany): Houseplant or interiorscape; landscape in flower gardens as tender, herbaceous annual' and 'Landscape Location: Container, Houseplants, Patio, ...'. I fetched the live page and confirmed these are genuine structured attribute fields, not prose. The record's unknowns section acknowledges this citation exists and dismisses it as 'genus-level' (the page's own Species field literally reads 'spp.'), but T. patula is one of the specific cultivars pictured/discussed on that same page, so the dismissal is a judgment call, not a settled fact — exactly the kind of genuine cross-source tension the audit instructions say should default to null rather than a confident false.

records.name_note: Ipomoea alba is the currently accepted name. NC State Extension lists Calonyction aculeatum and Ipomoea bona-nox as "previously known as" synonyms, and RHS lists this name's status as "Correct" (i.e. not itself a synonym).
records.toxicity_detail: Seeds are the toxic part (source names no other part). NC State rates it "low severity" under "Poisonous to Humans": symptoms are vomiting, and large amounts of seeds may cause hallucinations, from indole alkaloids (lysergic acid, lysergamide, elymoclavine, chanoclavine); it does not cause contact dermatitis. The same source separately tags the plant "a problem for cats, dogs, and horses" but gives no pet-specific symptom detail beyond that tag.

water_regime — removed on audit: The record asserts water_regime = 'keep_moist' citing only MOBOT's prose 'grown as an annual in moist, well-drained soils.' But I fetched the raw MOBOT page and confirmed it carries its own dedicated structured attribute field, printed right alongside the 'Sun: Full sun' line the record DID cite for outdoor_sun_exposure: 'Water: Medium'. This is a distinct, source-native rating that the record never quotes, cites, or reconciles, and 'Medium' is not self-evidently the same thing as 'keep constantly moist' (MOBOT uses a Dry/Medium/Wet-style scale elsewhere, where 'Medium' is the middle/average category, not the wettest one). This is exactly the 'structured field vs. quoted prose' conflict the audit brief specifically instructs checking for on harm-capable fields -- the record picked a value from one part of the source while ignoring a directly conflicting structured field on the same page. Should be null or should surface the conflict rather than asserting keep_moist outright.

records.name_note: Ipomoea purpurea is the currently accepted binomial. RHS lists its Name Status as "Correct," and Missouri Botanical Garden notes it is "Synonymous with and formerly known as Convolvulus purpureus" — confirming Ipomoea purpurea, not the older Convolvulus name, as accepted. No source suggested a different current name, so scientific_name_accepted is copied over as identical to scientific_name_given.

chill_damage_f: RHS gives only a general hardiness rating (H1C: 'can be grown outside in the summer (5-10°C)'), which is a zone/survival classification, not an actionable frost-damage-onset temperature, so left null per the field's definition.
humidity_need/humidity_pct_min/humidity_pct_max: not addressed by any admissible source.
light_fc_min/light_fc_good: no source gives a footcandle value; only the qualitative 'full sun' category is stated, captured instead in outdoor_sun_exposure.

direct_sun_hours_max: NC State's 'full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day)' is generic site-wide boilerplate defining NC State's 'full sun' category, not a species-specific figure, so not used as a numeric value.

soil_ph_min/soil_ph_max: NC State and RHS both list this species as tolerant of Acid, Alkaline, and Neutral soil, but neither gives a specific numeric pH boundary beyond the category names, so no defensible min/max number exists.
fertilize_active_months/fertilize_interval_days/fertilize_strength: no admissible source addresses fertilizing this species.

water_growing_days_est/water_dormant_days_est/water_check_depth_cm/water_dry_down_target/water_estimate_basis: sources describe moisture qualitatively ('consistently moist, well-drained') but give no watering interval, check-depth, or day-count data to base an estimate on.
cool_rest_note: not addressed by any admissible source.

soil_base/soil_drainage are inferred categorical readings (garden_bed; moderate) from qualitative planting-location and drainage-tag text rather than an exact enum-label match in the source text; flagged here in case a stricter reading would prefer null.

toxicity_detail — removed on audit: The severity/symptom/mechanism content is misattributed across target organism. NC State's page (confirmed by direct fetch) has two distinct sections: 'Poisonous to Humans' (Poison Severity: Low; Poison Symptoms: Vomiting, large amounts of seeds may cause hallucinations; Poison Toxic Principle: Indole alkaloids...) and a separate 'Problems:' section (Problem for Cats / Problem for Dogs / Problem for Horses / Weedy) that carries NO severity, symptom, mechanism, or plant-part detail at all. Citation #3's own quote literally begins with the words 'Poisonous to Humans:' yet its claim label repurposes that human-toxicology content to support toxic_to_pets/toxicity_detail. The UGA citation (#14) is the same problem one level worse: I fetched the actual PDF and its table is titled 'Ornamental Plants Reported To Be Toxic When Ingested by HUMANS' (confirmed on p.3 of the PDF) -- it is not a pet/animal toxicity table at all, on top of already being genus-level (Ipomoea spp.), which the record does disclose but the human-vs-pet mismatch it does not. As a result, toxicity_detail's lead sentence 'Seeds are the specifically implicated toxic part' is not established by any source that actually addresses pet toxicity -- the two sources that do speak to pets (RHS 'Pets: Harmful if eaten' and NC State's Problem-for-Cats/Dogs/Horses tags) name no plant part and no severity at all. The seed-specific attribution and the 'Low' severity rating are both imported wholesale from human-poisoning data without disclosing that gap, which is exactly the kind of over-reach the audit is meant to catch given seeds' well-documented toxicity/psychoactivity in this genus. toxic_to_pets=true itself is fine (independently supported by RHS's explicit pets line and NC State's Problem tags), but the elaborated toxicity_detail overstates what is actually known about the pet-specific picture.

water_regime — removed on audit: This is the 'structured field contradicts the prose quote' trap the audit specifically warns about. I fetched the live MoBot page and its structured 'Growing Conditions' summary reads: Sun: Full sun / Water: Medium / Maintenance: Low -- MoBot's own middle/average moisture tier, not their wettest category. The record's citation #7 quotes only the prose culture line ('consistently moist, well-drained soils,' which is MoBot's standard boilerplate phrasing for plants in its Water:Medium tier) and on that basis alone settles on water_regime = keep_moist, without ever surfacing or reconciling MoBot's own 'Water: Medium' structured rating on the very same page. RHS's structured 'Moisture: Moist but well-drained' field (citation #11) is internally consistent with the RHS prose quoted, but 'moist but well-drained' is RHS's default/most-common moisture category for ordinary garden plants and does not resolve the tension with MoBot's explicitly moderate 'Medium' rating for this same species -- a genuine unflagged cross-source disagreement on a harm-capable field.

records.name_note: RHS explicitly lists this binomial's Name Status as "Correct." Separately, NC State's Plant Toolbox page for this species lists "Watercress" among Tropaeolum majus's common names and also shows a "Previously known as: Nasturtium officinale" synonym line — this looks like a common-name cross-reference artifact on NC State's own page (both plants share the common thread "nasturtium/watercress" and a peppery edible taste) rather than a stated taxonomic synonymy, since no admissible source asserts the two binomials are the same plant. Accepted name was therefore not changed from the given name.
unknowns: day_f_min/day_f_max and night_f_min/night_f_max: no admissible source gives explicit daytime or nighttime temperature values for this species.

chill_damage_f: RHS gives an H3 hardiness rating ("hardy in coastal and relatively mild parts of the UK (-5 to 1)" degrees C), but per the task's own instruction that is a hardiness-zone/survival-tolerance rating for a mature/established planting, not a stated frost-damage-onset temperature, so it was not used.
humidity_need, humidity_pct_min, humidity_pct_max: no admissible source addresses ambient humidity for this species.

light_fc_min, light_fc_good, direct_sun_hours_max: all cited sources give only a sun-duration category (full sun / partial shade / semi-shade), never a footcandle value or an explicit maximum-hours figure.

soil_ph_min/soil_ph_max: NC State's structured Soil pH field has Acid (<6.0), Neutral (6.0-8.0), and Alkaline (>8.0) all checked (i.e. no real numeric boundary is implied), and RHS structured field likewise says pH "Acid or Alkaline or Neutral"; Missouri Botanical Garden's prose separately describes a preference for soil that is "slightly acidic" but gives no number. No usable numeric range could be extracted.

water_regime: genuine cross-source tension, left null rather than resolved. Missouri Botanical Garden's own structured field reads "Water: Medium" while its own prose says plants "have some tolerance for dry soils"; NC State independently tags the species '#drought tolerant' and '#dry soils tolerant' and states in prose it is "tolerant of both drought and neglect"; but University of Maryland Extension (whose page is titled generically "Tropaeolum sp.", not confirmed as T. majus specifically) says nasturtiums "should be kept watered during the hottest, driest part of the summer." No source's wording maps cleanly onto one of the water_regime categories, and the sources pull in different directions on how much drought stress is advisable, so this was left null per the harm-capable-field rule.
water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, water_estimate_basis: no source gives a watering interval in days, and water_regime itself is unresolved, so no day-count estimate was made.

fertilize_interval_days, fertilize_strength, fertilize_active_months: NC State ("Fertilizing will increase foliage, however, will also decrease flowering.") and Missouri Botanical Garden ("Avoid fertilization which tends to increase foliage output but decrease flower production.") both advise minimizing/avoiding fertilizer, but neither gives an application rate, interval, or month range that would populate these fields.

toxicity_detail: NC State's structured 'Problems:' field flags 'Problem for Cats', 'Problem for Dogs', and 'Problem for Horses' for this species, but the page gives no toxic compound, plant part, or symptom detail beyond the tag itself, and no other admissible source addresses animal toxicity for this species at all (RHS's 'Potentially harmful' note is specifically about human skin contact/handling, not animals, so it neither corroborates nor conflicts).

is_houseplant — removed on audit: Value is false, but the record's own citation admits the basis is silence, not a statement: 'no source describes indoor cultivation.' The quoted NC State text ('It is popular in various types of gardens') only describes outdoor garden popularity — it never says the species is unsuited to indoor growing. This is exactly the pattern the audit's structural check #3 warns about: a negative claim (is_houseplant=false) manufactured from absence of evidence and presented as a settled field value rather than left null or hedged.

outdoor_sun_exposure — removed on audit: One of the three citations behind full_sun/part_shade is University of Maryland Extension's page, which is titled generically 'Tropaeolum sp.' and covers the genus rather than confirming T. majus specifically — a fact the record itself flags as a reason to distrust that same UMD source for water_regime, but does not flag when reusing it here. The final full_sun+part_shade value happens to still be corroborated independently by NC State and RHS, so the value survives, but citing an admittedly non-species-confirmed source as plain supporting evidence in one field while treating it as suspect in another is an inconsistent evidentiary standard the record doesn't disclose.

unknowns: toxic_to_pets: none of the eight approved-domain sources checked (NC State, Clemson, Missouri Botanical Garden, UF/IFAS, RHS, Penn State, UGA) address toxicity of Viola x wittrockiana to cats/dogs. NC State notes the flowers are edible for humans (with a pesticide-residue caution) but that does not establish pet safety either way, so left null rather than inferring from the Violaceae family.

water_regime: genuine cross-source conflict. NC State ('consistently moist and well-drained' soil, structured Soil Drainage tags 'Good Drainage'/'Moist') and Clemson (water whenever <1in rain falls per week, ~1in/week in spring) describe a moisture-loving regime, while UGA's landscape-professional guide gives an explicit overwatering warning ('cannot tolerate wet feet') and instructs keeping plants 'slightly on the dry side' before cold snaps. Left null rather than picking a side, per the harm-capable-field rule.

fertilize_interval_days: sources disagree substantially on frequency, not just wording. UGA's professional bed program uses a 15-2-20 liquid feed every 14 days through March 15; Clemson's home-garden guidance uses a granular 5-10-10 applied only twice a year (late fall and early spring). Left null rather than presenting either as the general answer.

day_f_min/day_f_max and night_f_min/night_f_max: no cited source gives an ambient air day/night temperature range for pansy. UGA gives only a SOIL temperature target for planting ('soil temperatures between 45° F and 65° F for best growth'), a different measurement not mapped onto these fields.
light_fc_min/light_fc_good: outdoor sources (NC State, Missouri Botanical Garden, RHS) give only a sun-exposure duration category (full sun to part shade), never a footcandle figure.

direct_sun_hours_max: NC State's 'Full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day)' tag gives a minimum threshold for the full-sun category, not an upper limit; no source states a maximum recommended hours of direct sun for this sun-tolerant species.
humidity_need/humidity_pct_min/humidity_pct_max: not addressed by any cited source for this outdoor bedding annual.

soil_base: sources describe organically enriched garden/bed soil generally (Clemson: add manure, leaf mold, or compost) but pansies are grown both in-ground and in containers per these same sources, and none specifies a potting-mix category cleanly matching one soil_base enum value, so left null.

fertilize_active_months/fertilize_strength: sources give only relative timing ('late fall', 'early spring', 'through March 15') and NPK ratios/ppm, not calendar month numbers or a fraction-of-full-strength dilution, so left null rather than inventing precision.

cool_rest_note: not addressed. Sources describe cold-survival and cold-damage thresholds for an outdoor annual (e.g., UGA: survives 'down to the single digits, freezing solid, then bouncing back'), not a houseplant-style dormancy/rest period, so this field does not apply cleanly and was left null.

water_check_depth_cm/water_growing_days_est/water_dormant_days_est/water_dry_down_target/water_estimate_basis: left null because water_regime itself is null due to a genuine source conflict; populating day-count estimates or a dry-down target without an underlying regime would misrepresent that disagreement.

RHS species-level profile page for Viola x wittrockiana (plant ID 156646) returned a 404/certificate error on every fetch attempt; only an individual cultivar series page (Matrix Series) on rhs.org.uk was reachable and is cited only for corroborating, non-cultivar-specific sun-exposure and soil-texture claims that matched the species-level sources.

soil_drainage — removed on audit: Value 'moderate' is not stated anywhere. The NC State quote used says only 'consistently moist and well-drained' — never 'moderate.' Worse, the record's own unknowns section (water_regime entry) quotes NC State's own STRUCTURED Soil Drainage tag as 'Good Drainage'/'Moist' — a self-contradiction inside the same record. 'Good Drainage' does not map to 'moderate'; the record invented an intermediate value that contradicts both the quoted prose and the source's own structured field.

name_note — removed on audit: Claims 'NC State, Missouri Botanical Garden, and RHS all use this binomial for the garden pansy.' The only RHS citation in the record is a sun-exposure quote ('Full sun, Partial shade') from a specific cultivar page (Viola wittrockiana Matrix Series) — the quote never states the scientific name, and the page's own URL/title omits the hybrid marker entirely ('viola-wittrockiana-matrix-series', no x or ×). Nothing in the citations actually shows RHS using 'Viola × wittrockiana.' The naming claim for RHS is unsupported by any quote in the record.

outdoor_sun_exposure — removed on audit: The RHS citation offered as corroboration is for a single cultivar series (Matrix Series), not a species-level profile — a genus/cultivar-vs-species specificity problem (check #2). The record's own unknowns note acknowledges the true RHS species page (plant ID 156646) was unreachable and substitutes the cultivar page, but the citation label still presents it as 'corroborating' species-level evidence without flagging that it is cultivar-specific. The field value itself is fine on NC State + MBG alone, but this citation shouldn't be represented as species-level support.

records.name_note: RHS's own species-group page lists "Petunia × atkinsiana" with Name Status "Correct" and gives "Petunia × hybrida" as a Synonym; a cultivar page titled "Petunia × hybrida 'Storm Lavender'" is itself marked Name Status "Synonym" on RHS. NC State Extension and Missouri Botanical Garden, by contrast, both use "Petunia x hybrida" as their working name and do not flag it as a synonym. Given RHS's explicit synonym/name-status fields, scientific_name_accepted is set to Petunia x atkinsiana; this is copied from RHS's stated accepted name, not constructed by combining parent species.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State Extension's Plant Toolbox tags Petunia x hybrida as non-toxic to cats, dogs, and horses; no additional detail on compound or ingestion effects is given.
unknowns: water_regime: sources genuinely disagree — NC State rates it 'moderate drought tolerance' and tags it #drought tolerant, while Missouri Botanical Garden's own structured Water field says 'Medium' (not low/drought-tolerant) and describes 'average, medium moisture' soil, and UGA CAES says it 'require[s] ample moisture ... to thrive'. Left null rather than resolving the conflict.

chill_damage_f: no cited source gives a specific frost-damage-onset temperature; sources only describe it qualitatively (tender/half-hardy, hardy to USDA zones 10-11, plant after frost danger passes). An RHS cultivar page separately gives an H2 hardiness rating (1-5C) for one specific cultivar, but that is a mature-plant survival/tolerance floor, not a damage-onset temperature, and is cultivar- not species-level, so it was not used.

day_f_min/day_f_max/night_f_min/night_f_max: no source gives an ambient day/night growing-temperature range for established outdoor plants. NC State's 72-75F figure is specifically a seed-germination temperature, not a growing-temperature range, so it was not mapped to these fields.
humidity_need/humidity_pct_min/humidity_pct_max: not addressed by any cited source.

light_fc_min/light_fc_good/direct_sun_hours_max: sources give only a qualitative outdoor sun-exposure category (full sun to part shade), never a footcandle or hour-count value. NC State's '6 or more hours of direct sunlight' text is a generic definition of its site-wide 'Full sun' category label (reused across many plant pages), not a petunia-specific figure, so it was not used for direct_sun_hours_max.
fertilize_strength/fertilize_active_months: Clemson gives a monthly interval for fertilizing but does not state a dilution strength or specific calendar months.

soil_base: sources describe petunia used in garden beds/borders and in containers/hanging baskets about equally without specifying a distinct growing medium for either, so no single soil_base category is asserted.

water_check_depth_cm/water_dry_down_target/water_growing_days_est/water_dormant_days_est/water_estimate_basis: dependent on water_regime, which is null due to the source conflict noted above; no source gives a soil-check depth in any case.
cool_rest_note: not addressed by any cited source.

is_houseplant set false: NC State and Missouri Botanical Garden each mention occasional indoor overwintering of favorite/unique plants ('interior sunrooms in the winter, depending on the hybrid'; 'may be overwintered indoors in a bright cool location') but neither describes petunia as commonly grown indoors long-term, so this was not treated as houseplant support.

soil_drainage — removed on audit: The record sets soil_drainage to "moderate" citing Clemson's quote "Best growth occurs in well-drained, light soil of medium fertility" -- but the word/category "moderate" never appears in that quote; "well-drained" is not synonymous with a moderate-drainage rating. Worse, I re-fetched the very NC State Extension page that is cited elsewhere in this same record for other fields, and it carries its own dedicated structured field: "Soil Drainage: Good Drainage, Moist" -- a first-party structured rating that was never checked or cited, and that points to "Good Drainage," not "moderate." This is exactly the check-1 pattern: a cited source's own structured field was not checked before a value was picked, and the picked value ("moderate") isn't literally supported by either source's language.

fertilize_interval_days — removed on audit: The citation's claim label states "fertilize_interval_days 30," but the only quote backing it is Clemson's "Fertilize petunias monthly with a balanced fertilizer..." -- the digit 30 (or any spelled-out equivalent) never appears in the quote. "Monthly" was silently converted to an exact 30-day interval, which is a specific inserted number not present in the source, failing the audit's own re-derivation test (every number in a claim label must be literally traceable to the quote).

is_houseplant — removed on audit: is_houseplant is set to a definite false, but the only supporting citation is qualitative and self-hedging -- its own claim label reads "...no value taken for is_houseplant true," i.e., the citation itself frames this as unresolved, yet the top-level field was still populated with a confident false rather than left null. More importantly, re-fetching the cited NC State page turns up a structured Tags field the record never checked or cited: among the tags is "#interiorscape" (NC State's own indoor/interior-landscape-use tag), sitting alongside the prose about "interior sunrooms in the winter" that the record did quote. A false determination that ignores the source's own structured indoor-use tag, while quoting only the softer prose, is an absence of contrary evidence dressed up as a stated negative fact -- precisely the pattern structural check 3 asks to catch.

normalizations: 2026-08-21: landed with zero manual fixes. Two findings worth keeping in mind for future name-resolution work. Annual Geranium's scientific_name_accepted was set to Pelargonium x hybridum on a single source's say-so, but the audit fetched the record's other cited sources directly and found RHS explicitly rates the name status 'Unresolved' while Clemson, MOBOT and UF/IFAS all still use the given name (x hortorum) as their working name -- a genuine cross-source dispute, not a settled reclassification. Nulled, along with a name_note whose own final sentence contradicted the evidence it had just laid out. Petunia's resolution to Petunia x atkinsiana was left alone as a materially different situation: one source (RHS) makes an explicit accepted/synonym determination that the other sources are simply silent about, not actively disputing.

Common Morning Glory's toxicity handling separated two questions the source itself keeps apart: NC State's page has a distinct 'Poisonous to Humans' section (with mechanism and symptoms) and a separate, undetailed 'Problem for Cats/Dogs/Horses' tag. The record had cross-attributed the human section's specific content to toxicity_detail; the audit correctly stripped only that text, leaving toxic_to_pets=true standing on the tag that actually supports it. Nasturtium's toxic_to_pets=true rests on a bare but specific three-animal tag with no mechanism given -- thinner than most, but a different evidentiary situation from Kohlrabi's b10 case, where the tag named only an animal (horses) unrelated to the field's actual question and left cats/dogs unaddressed.
